body_markdown:
If you've ever looked down at your kid mid-show and wondered, *is it too loud in here?* Trust that instinct, because it's usually right. And most parents never think to ask.


The show that feels loud to you is louder for your kid. It's simple physics, and it has an easy fix.


Concerts, Monster Jam, fireworks, race day at the track. Each one crosses into ear damaging territory, and each calls for something a little different:


Event Recommended Protection


Concerts & festivals Muffs (under 6) or[MONSTER JAM earplugs](https://goaxil.com/collections/monster-jam) (6+)


Monster Jam Muffs (under 6) or[MONSTER JAM earplugs](https://goaxil.com/collections/monster-jam) (6+)


Fireworks Muffs, plus distance from the launch site


Stadium games Muffs (under 6) or[MONSTER JAM earplugs](https://goaxil.com/collections/monster-jam) (6+)


Shooting range AXIL ear muffs over plugs, doubled up


## Kids Need More Hearing Protection Than Adults Do


A child's ear canal is smaller and still developing, which raises the sound pressure hitting the eardrum at the exact same decibel level an adult standing right next to them is experiencing. Same show, same seat, harder hit.


### The Damage Is Cumulative and Permanent


Every loud event adds to a running total a child's ears carry for life. Loud noise damages the tiny hair cells inside the cochlea, and unlike a scraped knee, those cells never heal or regenerate. The damage builds up show by show with no outward sign, and a child rarely complains about it the way they'd complain about anything else that hurts. But the damage can show up years later, long after anyone remembers the events that caused it.


### 85 Decibels Is the Threshold to Know


None of that is meant to scare you off the next family outing. The number to know is 85 decibels (dB), the point where unprotected exposure time starts counting against a child's hearing, according to the[CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/hearing-loss-children/about/preventing-noise-induced-hearing-loss.html) and[NIDCD](https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/noise-induced-hearing-loss) . Concerts, Monster Jam, fireworks: most clear that threshold within minutes of the gates opening. A little preparation goes a long way.


### Watch for This One Warning Sign


If your child is covering their ears or telling you it's too loud, they've already crossed the safe limit. Treat that as your cue to have protection on *before* the show starts.


You know the 85-decibel limit sits. Next is how fast the events on your family's calendar reach it.


## How Loud Are Kids' Events? Here's the Decibel Breakdown


Monster Jam, concerts, fireworks, stadium games, air shows: all of it clears that 85 dB line, some by a wide margin. Fireworks alone can peak more than 60 decibels above it at close range.


### Decibel Levels by Event


Event Typical Level Peak Level Safe Exposure Time*


Movie theaters 75–85 dB 90–100 dB (action scenes) Hours typical; ~15 min during loud scenes


Stadium games 94–110 dB Up to 142 dB (crowd roar) ~2–60 min


Concerts & festivals 100–110 dB N/A ~2–15 min


Monster Jam 95–100 dB 120+ dB ~15–45 min


Motorsport grandstands 100–115 dB N/A ~30 sec–15 min


Air shows 110–120 dB N/A ~10 sec–2 min


Fireworks (close range) N/A 140–150 dB Seconds


These exposure times reflect NIOSH's 3-decibel exchange rate (every 3 dB increase cuts safe exposure roughly in half), applied across each event's dB range, from[CDC/NIOSH](https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/noise/prevent/understand.html) . Exact figures vary by venue, seating, and speaker placement.


### Do Kids Need Ear Protection at Loud Events?


Yes. Anything that holds 85 dB for a sustained stretch qualifies, and that covers nearly everything on your family's calendar this year. The fix from here is simple: match the protection to your kid's age first, then fine-tune for the event.


## The Right Ear Protection Changes as Your Kid Grows


Here’s a trusty rule of thumb for your kid’s ear protection: ear muffs win for kids under about 6, earplugs take over from there.


If you've ever tried to keep an earplug seated in a toddler's ear for more than ninety seconds, you already know why. Muffs never go into the canal, so there's nothing to insert wrong, and you can check the fit at a glance without asking a toddler to hold still (good luck with that).


A toddler also can't yank off a pair of muffs one-handed the way they can pop out a plug the second you look away. Earplugs become realistic once a child can seat one properly and tell you if something's off. For most kids, that's right around age 6.


### The Youngest Kids Need a Full Seal, Not Just Coverage


If your child is under 12 months, it’s probably best to skip the event entirely if you reasonably can. This is the one age where "just be careful" doesn't quite cover it. If it's unavoidable, look for infant-specific muffs rated NRR 25 or higher, and keep the visit short.


For toddlers, look for an adjustable headband and an NRR in the 22–27 range, then check for a full seal: no gaps where the cushion meets the head, not muffs just resting on top of the ears. The[American Academy of Pediatrics](https://www.aap.org/en/patient-care/environmental-health/promoting-healthy-environments-for-children/noise/) treats this as the hardest age range to get hearing protection right, which won't surprise anyone who's wrangled a two-year-old into anything they didn't pick out themselves.


Fit-test the muffs at home for a few minutes a day, two or three days before the event. The first time your toddler wears them shouldn't also be the loudest, most overwhelming moment of their day. Let them get bored of the muffs on the couch first, and they'll fight you a lot less in the stands.


A quick aside on airplanes: cabin noise usually stays below the level that risks damage on a single flight, though it can run close to that line, especially near the engines. Ear pressure during takeoff and landing is the more immediate concern day-to-day, and muffs won't touch it. A bottle, a pacifier, or just swallowing works better.


### "Noise-Cancelling" Isn't the Same as Hearing Protection


This is another challenge parents run into when looking for ear protection for their kids. When you look up "noise cancelling headphones for kids," brands usually mean passive ear muffs. True active noise-cancelling (ANC) headphones are a different product, built to cancel low-frequency hum electronically. They're not tested or rated as hearing protection, so don't count on a pair of ANC kids' headphones to do the job at a loud event.


### Ear Protection by Age at a Glance


With muffs, plugs, and that noise-cancelling mix-up covered, a quick reference as your kid grows:


Age Band Recommended Type NRR Range


Under 1 Infant muffs 25+


1–5 Toddler muffs 22–27


6–12 Fitted earplugs (muffs as fallback) Varies by product


Teens Adult earplugs or muffs Varies by product


## Kids Ear Protection, Matched to Every Age and Every Show


Choosing the actual earplugs for your kids comes down to two questions: how old is your kid, and can they manage it themselves? From age 6 up, fitted earplugs can protect your child’s hearing through concerts, Monster Jam, stadium games, race day, all of it. This is where[AXIL's Monster Jam line](https://goaxil.com/collections/monster-jam) was built to work.

Your kid doesn't have to choose between hearing safely and feeling like part of the show.


## The Right Ear Protection Setup for Concerts, Monster Jam, Fireworks, and the Range


The setup still changes a little depending on where you're headed:


### Concerts Hold Loud Sound Indoors for Hours


Concerts run one to three hours, indoors more often than not, with sound bouncing off walls and ceilings on top of what's already coming straight off the speakers. The exact number depends heavily on genre: a rock or pop show often lands around 100–110 dB, an orchestra or choir performance can sit closer to 70–90 dB, and a metal show can push past 115 dB.


Whatever's on the bill, it’s better to stay at the back third of the venue, away from the stacks, and grab an aisle seat so it’s easier to step out for a breather. One thing to know before you rely on it: the foam plugs some venues hand out at the door are sized for adults and rarely seal in a small ear canal. So if you’ve got a kid along, it’s better to bring your own. And while you're protecting your kid's hearing, don't skip your own. You're standing in the same room.[Here's what to bring for yourself](https://goaxil.com/blogs/axil/earplugs-for-concerts) .


Concerts are loud, but at least predictable. Monster Jam turns the volume up in a different way entirely.


### Monster Jam Sustains Damaging Noise for Two Hours Straight


Every kid at Monster Jam needs ear protection, no exceptions. Truck engines hold 95–100 dB for the entire two-plus-hour show, well past the point where unprotected exposure starts adding up, with spikes past 120 dB during jumps and freestyle runs


[AXIL is the official Monster Jam ear protection partner](https://goaxil.com/collections/monster-jam) , and the[X20](https://goaxil.com/products/monster-jam-x20-earplugs?_pos=1&_sid=757de8d41&_ss=r) and[X30i](https://goaxil.com/products/monster-jam-x30i-earplugs?_pos=2&_sid=757de8d41&_ss=r) were built specifically for this event, down to the truck-branded designs your kid will want to wear.


Sitting near the floor puts you closest to the peak noise, so[double up for younger kids: muffs over plugs.](https://goaxil.com/blogs/axil/doubling-up-with-plugs-and-muffs) If motorsports go beyond just Monster Jam for your family, the[complete motorsport ear protection guide](https://goaxil.com/blogs/axil/best-ear-protection-for-nascar-and-motorsport-events-a-complete-guide) covers NASCAR and local tracks in more depth.


That's sustained engine noise for two hours straight. Fireworks flip the problem: instead of a steady roar, it's one massive burst.


### Fireworks Peak at 140–150 dB, the Loudest Night of the Year


Fireworks get treated like the gentlest event on this list: a blanket, some snacks, a nice night out. In reality, they produce some of the most dangerous noise your kid will face all year: impulse peaks of 140–150 dB at close range, according to the[American Academy of Pediatrics](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/news/Pages/sounds-the-alarm-on-excessive-noise-and-risks-to-children.aspx) .


The[World Health Organization](https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/documents/health-topics/deafness-and-hearing-loss/monograph-on-noise-exposure-limit-for-children-in-recreational-settings.pdf) sets its recommended limit specifically for children at 120 dB, a full 20 decibels below the adult limit, because a child's ears take a harder hit at the same volume.


One fix costs nothing: put more distance between your family and the launch site. Pair that with muffs and you've covered the loudest night of their year without much extra effort at all.


Distance handles fireworks. The range calls for something stricter.


### The Range Demands Doubled-Up Protection


This is AXIL's home turf, and the rule here is stricter than anywhere else on this list, for good reason. Gunfire produces impulse noise up to 175 dB depending on caliber, past what any single layer of protection can fully block on its own. Muffs go over plugs for kids at the range.


For older kids who are shooting or standing the line, electronic muffs are worth the upgrade: they amplify speech-level sound like range commands and your voice, while still clipping gunshot-level peaks before they reach the ear. It's the same Protect + Enhance idea behind the[X30i](https://goaxil.com/products/monster-jam-x30i-earplugs?_pos=2&_sid=757de8d41&_ss=r) , just built for a louder, higher-stakes environment. The[ear muffs collection](https://goaxil.com/collections/ear-muffs) fits best once a child has grown into an adult-small size, and the[doubling-up guide](https://goaxil.com/blogs/axil/doubling-up-with-plugs-and-muffs) walks through the full setup.


## Kids Ear Protection FAQ: Quick Answers for Busy Parents


What NRR should kids ear protection have?


22 or higher for general events, 25 or higher for infants and impulse noise like fireworks and gunfire.


At what age can kids use earplugs instead of muffs?


Around age 6, once they can seat a plug correctly on their own and tell you if something feels off.


Do babies need ear protection on airplanes?


For comfort and sleep, yes. A single flight usually stays below the level that risks hearing damage, though cabin noise can run close to that line, especially near the engines. The more immediate issue during takeoff and landing is ear pressure, and muffs won't help with that part.


Do kids need ear protection at Monster Jam?


Yes. Sustained sound holds at 95–100 dB for more than two hours, well past the safe exposure window at that level.


Can kids wear adult earplugs?


Usually not comfortably, though it comes down to fit more than age. Adult plugs are sized for adult canals, and most kids' ears don't grow into that size until closer to the teen years. Kid-sized tips are what make the seal work in the meantime.


How do I know ear muffs are sealing properly?


No visible gap where the cushion meets the head, a snug (not loose) headband, and a second check any time a hat or hairstyle changes the fit during the day.


With the specifics covered, there's one thing worth remembering before the next show.


## What to Remember Before Your Kid's Next Loud Event


Concerts, Monster Jam, fireworks, the shooting range: every one of them clears the safe noise threshold for a child's ears. The damage is real and permanent. The fix is small, affordable, and easier than it sounds once you know what to look for.


If you remember nothing else: muffs until your kid can manage plugs on their own, plugs once they can, doubled-up protection for gunfire and front-row noise. From there, it's just matching the product to your kid's age and the event ahead, then getting back to enjoying it together.
